title: Inventories
outcomes: Explain what counts as inventory for a trader and a manufacturer, and what does not.
Explain why the inventory figure affects profit, the balance sheet, liquidity ratios and statutory disclosure.
Apply "lower of cost and net realisable value" — working out cost (what to include and exclude) and NRV, item by item.
Distinguish the periodic and perpetual inventory systems.
Value inventory by specific identification, FIFO, simple and weighted average, adjusted selling price and standard cost, and explain why LIFO is not allowed.
Work back or forward from a physical count taken on a date other than the balance sheet date, dealing with goods on approval and goods held on consignment.

meta.exam_tip: Expect a 4–6 mark computation (FIFO / weighted average stores ledger or inventory on the balance sheet date) and short theory on cost vs NRV or periodic vs perpetual. Always state the basis — "lower of cost and NRV".

concepts.title: What inventory is
body: Inventory means assets that are (a) held for sale in the normal course of business, (b) in the process of being produced for such sale, or (c) materials and supplies to be used up in producing goods or rendering services. Maintenance supplies and consumables are included.

A trader's inventory is mainly goods bought for resale in the same form, plus small supplies such as cartons and wrapping material. A manufacturer holds raw materials, work-in-progress (partly finished goods), finished goods, stores and spares, loose tools and packing material. For a construction business, projects under construction are inventory too.

Not inventory: machinery spares, servicing equipment and standby equipment that can be used only with a particular item of plant and whose use is irregular — these are treated as fixed assets (property, plant and equipment). Goods held for someone else (for example on consignment) are not your inventory either.
concepts.analogy: Think of a bakery: flour in the store (raw material), dough in the oven (WIP), bread on the shelf (finished goods). The oven itself is not inventory — it is a fixed asset.
concepts.work: In a stock audit, the first question is ownership: are the goods in the godown really the client's? Third-party goods are a common source of overstated inventory.

concepts.title: Why the inventory figure matters so much
body: Profit: cost of goods sold is worked out as opening inventory plus purchases and direct expenses, minus closing inventory. Closing inventory overstated → profit overstated; closing understated → profit understated. Opening inventory overstated → profit understated; opening understated → profit overstated. The error always flows through cost of goods sold, and this year's closing becomes next year's opening, so an error reverses next year.

Financial position and liquidity: inventory is usually the largest current asset. A wrong figure distorts the balance sheet, working capital and the current ratio (current assets ÷ current liabilities) that bankers rely on. Slow-moving or non-moving items are often the hidden cause of weak results.

Statutory disclosure: Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013 requires inventories to be shown class-wise (raw materials, work-in-progress, finished goods, stock-in-trade, stores and spares, loose tools), and accounting standards require disclosure of the accounting policy and the cost formula used.

head: If this is overstated…
Profit for the year is…
blocks.note: Understatement has exactly the opposite effects.

concepts.analogy: Closing inventory is the bridge between two years — if you shift the bridge, one bank of the river looks bigger and the other smaller.
concepts.work: Inflating closing stock is one of the oldest ways to dress up profit. That is why auditors attend the physical count and banks insist on monthly stock statements for working-capital loans.

concepts.title: Basis: lower of cost and net realisable value
body: Inventories are measured at cost or net realisable value (NRV), whichever is lower. This follows prudence (conservatism): an expected loss is recognised at once, while an expected profit is not recognised until the goods are sold.
If selling prices have fallen below cost, writing the goods down to NRV books the loss in the year it becomes evident, not in the year of sale.

The comparison is normally made item by item. Similar or related items that cannot practically be valued separately may be grouped. Comparing total cost with total NRV is not the normal approach, because a gain on one item would hide a loss on another.

concepts.analogy: A shopkeeper prices yesterday's bread at what it will actually fetch today, if that is less than what it cost — but never marks fresh bread up to its selling price before it is sold.
concepts.work: At year-end, accountants run an "NRV test": compare each item's cost with recent or expected selling prices less selling costs, and provide for expired, damaged or obsolete stock.

concepts.title: What goes into cost — and what stays out
body: Cost = costs of purchase + costs of conversion + other costs incurred to bring the goods to their present location and condition.

Costs of purchase: purchase price, import duties and taxes that cannot be recovered later, freight inward, handling and other costs directly linked to acquiring the goods, less trade discounts, rebates and duty drawbacks. GST for which input credit is available is not cost.

Costs of conversion: direct labour and a systematic share of fixed and variable production overheads. Other costs: for example design cost for a specific customer, or administrative overheads that clearly help bring goods to their present condition. Interest is generally excluded, but may be included where goods need a long time to get ready for sale (wine, rice, timber).

Excluded: abnormal wastage of material, labour or overheads (normal wastage stays in cost); storage costs, unless storage is a necessary step in production (for example ageing wine); administrative overheads that do not help bring goods to their present location and condition; selling and distribution costs.

blocks.title: Step 1 — cost of finished product A

concepts.analogy: Cost is everything you spent to get the product onto your shelf, ready to sell — not what you spend afterwards to sell it, and not what you lost through an accident.
concepts.work: Cost-accounting teams prepare "inventory costing sheets" every quarter. Auditors test whether abnormal scrap or idle time has been wrongly loaded into stock values, which would inflate profit.

concepts.title: Net realisable value
body: NRV = the selling price you expect to get in the ordinary course of business, minus the further costs needed to complete the goods, minus the costs needed to make the sale.

Finished and traded goods: expected selling price less selling and distribution expenses. Work-in-progress: expected selling price of the finished product less costs to complete and costs to sell. Raw materials: replacement cost is generally used as the measure. (Under the accounting standard, materials are not written down at all if the finished goods they go into are expected to sell at or above cost — you will study this at the Intermediate level.)
NRV is assessed afresh at each balance sheet date.
concepts.analogy: NRV is the cash the item will actually bring home: price tag minus whatever you still have to spend to finish it and sell it.
concepts.work: In seasonal businesses (garments, electronics) NRV write-downs at year-end can be large; management estimates are reviewed against post-year-end sales.

concepts.title: Periodic and perpetual inventory systems
body: Periodic system: quantities are found by an actual physical count (or weighing/measuring) on the valuation date; cost of goods sold is the balancing figure: opening + purchases − closing. Simple and cheap, used by small businesses. Limitations: counting more than once a year is costly; operations may have to stop during counting; losses from theft, damage or fraud are hidden in cost of goods sold; no continuous control; the books do not tell you what is in stock at any moment.

Perpetual system: a stores ledger is updated after every receipt and issue, so cost of goods sold is known directly and closing inventory is the balancing figure in the books. It is costlier but gives continuous information and control. Physical checks are still needed to confirm the book balances; any shortage then shows up.
The two are complementary, not exclusive — most businesses keep perpetual records and verify them by periodic counts.

concepts.analogy: Periodic is checking how much milk is left by opening the fridge on Sunday; perpetual is writing down every glass you pour.
concepts.work: ERP systems (Tally, SAP) run perpetual inventory. Auditors still perform test counts and investigate book-vs-physical differences.

concepts.title: Cost formulas based on historical cost
body: Specific identification: the actual cost of each item is tracked. Used for items that are not ordinarily interchangeable or are made for specific projects — cars by chassis number, jewellery, custom machines.
FIFO (first in, first out): the earliest goods are assumed to be issued first, so closing inventory consists of the latest purchases. Same answer under periodic and perpetual records.

LIFO (last in, first out): the latest goods are assumed to be issued first, so closing inventory is valued at the oldest prices. It rarely matches the physical flow, gives different results under periodic and perpetual records, and leaves very old costs in the balance sheet. Accounting standards do not permit LIFO.

Simple average: the average of the different purchase prices, ignoring quantities — easy, but unrealistic when lot sizes differ. Weighted average: total cost of goods available ÷ total units available. Under periodic records one rate is worked out for the period; under perpetual records a new average is calculated after each receipt and used for the issues that follow. FIFO and weighted average are the formulas generally used in practice.

concepts.analogy: FIFO is a queue at a ticket counter; LIFO is a stack of plates — you take the top one, the one placed last.
concepts.work: A change in cost formula changes profit, so it is a change in accounting policy that must be justified and disclosed. Clients choosing between FIFO and weighted average in software need to understand this before the first entry.

concepts.title: Non-historical methods: adjusted selling price and standard cost
body: Adjusted selling price (retail) method: used by retailers with many fast-moving items with similar margins, where tracking individual cost is impractical. Closing inventory is counted at selling price and the gross margin percentage is deducted. Margin % = (selling value of goods available − cost of goods available) ÷ selling value of goods available. The percentage should allow for goods marked down below their original price; an average rate per department is common.

Standard cost method: inventory is valued at a pre-set standard cost per unit, based on experience, where prices change very frequently (for example crude oil). Standards must be reviewed regularly so that they stay close to actual cost.

concepts.analogy: A supermarket counts tins by their price stickers and then knocks off its usual margin to get back to cost.
concepts.work: Large retail chains value stock this way at store level; auditors test the margin percentage used and the effect of markdowns and promotions.

concepts.title: Inventory taking and adjusting to the balance sheet date
body: Physical counting is ideally done on the last day of the year. Often it is done a few days before or after; the counted figure is then adjusted to the balance sheet date for goods that came in or went out in between.

Count after the year-end: add back the cost of goods sold in the gap (net of sales returns, converted to cost) and deduct purchases received (and add back purchase returns). Count before the year-end: the reverse — add purchases, deduct purchase returns and the cost of net sales.

Goods sent on sale-or-return (approval) basis remain the sender's inventory, at cost, until the customer approves or the approval period ends — even though they are not in the godown. Goods received on consignment belong to the consignor (principal); the consignee (agent) holds them but must exclude them from its own inventory. Every item is still measured at the lower of cost and NRV.

concepts.work: Auditors attending a count carry out "cut-off" tests: the last goods received note and dispatch note before the year-end are matched to the books so that goods in transit are neither counted twice nor missed.

illustrations.title: FIFO, weighted average and simple average on the same data
illustrations.q: Ananya Lighting deals in LED panels. April 2026: Apr 1 opening 200 units @ ₹150; Apr 5 purchased 300 @ ₹160; Apr 9 issued 350; Apr 15 purchased 250 @ ₹172; Apr 22 issued 200; Apr 28 purchased 100 @ ₹180. solution.text: Goods available = 850 units costing ₹1,39,000. Rate = 1,39,000 ÷ 850 = ₹163.53. Closing 300 units × ₹163.53 ≈ ₹49,059.

solution.text: (150 + 160 + 172 + 180) ÷ 4 = ₹165.5; 300 × 165.5 = ₹49,650. Quantities are ignored, which is why this method is rarely acceptable when lot sizes differ.

jobs.title: Attending a year-end stock count
jobs.role: Articled assistant on a statutory audit of a manufacturer
jobs.situation: The client counts stock on 3 April. While observing, you notice (i) a stack of cartons marked with another company's name, (ii) dusty finished goods of a discontinued model, and (iii) a truck being unloaded in the middle of the count.
steps: Note the last goods received note and dispatch note numbers before the year-end and before the count (cut-off).
Ask about the third-party cartons — if held for a principal or on job work, they must be excluded from the client's inventory.
Record the discontinued model separately; later compare its cost with recent selling prices to see whether a write-down to NRV is needed.
Make sure goods unloaded during the count are either kept aside or counted and the receipt is excluded when rolling the count back to 31 March.
Perform test counts in both directions — floor to records and records to floor.
jobs.takeaway: Existence, ownership, cut-off and valuation — the four questions behind every inventory figure.
jobs.think: The count on 3 April shows ₹10.4 lakh. Purchases received 1–3 April are ₹0.9 lakh and sales 1–3 April are ₹1.2 lakh at a 20% margin on sales. What is the inventory on 31 March?

jobs.title: Setting up inventory valuation for a pharmacy
jobs.role: Accountant helping a client move to accounting software
jobs.situation: A pharmacy owner wants to "value stock at MRP because that is what is printed on the box". Some medicines expire within three months.
steps: Explain that inventory is carried at the lower of cost and NRV — never at selling price (MRP) before sale.
Set the software to weighted average (or FIFO); batch-wise tracking is useful because expiry follows batches.
Exclude GST for which input credit is available from cost; include freight inward.
At each month-end, run an expiry report and write down near-expiry or expired stock to its realisable value (often nil).
Disclose the cost formula used in the accounts.
jobs.takeaway: Valuing stock at selling price books profit before the sale happens — exactly what prudence forbids.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT inventory?
options: Standby equipment usable only with a particular machine and used irregularly
Raw materials in the factory store
mcqs.explain: Such spares and standby equipment are treated as property, plant and equipment, not inventory.

options: Lower of cost and net realisable value
Cost or market price, whichever is higher
mcqs.explain: Prudence: expected losses are recognised, expected gains are not.

mcqs.q: Which cost is included in the cost of inventory?
options: Rent of the warehouse for finished goods (routine storage)
mcqs.explain: Freight inward brings the goods to their present location; the others are excluded.

mcqs.q: Goods bought for ₹50,000 plus GST ₹9,000 (input credit available) and freight inward ₹1,500. Cost of inventory is:
mcqs.explain: Recoverable GST is excluded; freight inward is included: 50,000 + 1,500 = ₹51,500.

mcqs.q: Expected selling price ₹80,000; cost to complete ₹6,000; selling costs ₹4,000. NRV is:
Item X: cost ₹20,000, NRV ₹24,000. Item Y: cost ₹15,000, NRV ₹11,000. Inventory value is:
mcqs.explain: Item by item: X at 20,000 + Y at 11,000 = ₹31,000.

mcqs.q: Which cost formula is NOT permitted by the accounting standards?
mcqs.explain: LIFO leaves outdated costs in the balance sheet and rarely reflects the physical flow; it is not allowed.

mcqs.q: If closing inventory of the current year is overstated, the current year's profit is:
options: Overstated only if opening inventory is also overstated
mcqs.explain: Higher closing inventory lowers cost of goods sold and raises profit.

mcqs.q: If opening inventory is understated, profit for the year is:
mcqs.explain: Lower opening inventory lowers cost of goods sold, so profit is overstated.

mcqs.q: Under the periodic inventory system, loss of goods by theft is:
options: Hidden in cost of goods sold
Shown separately in the stores ledger
mcqs.explain: Cost of goods sold is a balancing figure, so anything missing is treated as sold.

mcqs.q: Opening 100 units @ ₹10; purchased 200 @ ₹13; 180 units sold. Closing inventory under FIFO is:
Opening 100 units @ ₹10; purchased 200 @ ₹13; 180 units sold. Closing inventory under periodic weighted average is:
Sales ₹4,00,000; closing inventory at selling price ₹1,00,000; cost of goods available ₹3,75,000. Closing inventory under the adjusted selling price method:
Goods sent on sale-or-return basis and not yet approved at the year-end are:
options: Included in the sender's inventory at cost
Treated as sales at selling price
mcqs.explain: Ownership has not passed, so they stay in the sender's inventory at the lower of cost and NRV.

mcqs.q: Specific identification is the appropriate method for:
options: Items not ordinarily interchangeable, such as custom-built machines
Retail stores with thousands of items
Crude oil with frequently changing prices
mcqs.explain: Specific identification fits unique or project-specific items whose individual cost can be traced.

Prepare the stores ledger and find the value of closing inventory under (a) FIFO and (b) weighted average (perpetual).

model.title: Answer
model.text: Closing inventory: FIFO 50 units @ ₹58 = ₹2,900; weighted average 50 units @ ₹56.75 = ₹2,837.5.

Weighted average: new rates ₹53 and ₹56.75 after each receipt

remarks: Many candidates worked out a single periodic average for the whole quarter although perpetual records were asked for.
Stores ledgers without a running balance column lost presentation marks.
mistakes: Recomputing the weighted average after an issue — the rate changes only after a receipt.
Under FIFO, issuing from the latest lot.
tips: Keep three blocks of columns: Receipts | Issues | Balance.
Write FIFO balances as layers (e.g. 100 @ 55) so the next issue is easy to price.

The product sells at ₹300 per unit with selling costs of ₹20 per unit. At what value should the inventory be shown?

summary: Inventory = held for sale, in production for sale, or materials/supplies to be consumed in production or services.
Valued at the lower of cost and NRV, normally item by item (prudence).
Cost = purchase + conversion + other costs to bring goods to present location and condition; exclude abnormal waste, routine storage, unrelated admin, selling and distribution, recoverable taxes.
NRV = expected selling price − costs to complete − costs to sell.
Periodic: COGS is the balancing figure. Perpetual: closing inventory is the balancing figure.
Formulas: specific identification, FIFO, weighted average (allowed); simple average (crude); LIFO (not permitted); adjusted selling price and standard cost (non-historical).
remember: Closing inventory overstated → profit overstated; opening overstated → profit understated.
Perpetual weighted average: recompute the rate after every receipt, not after issues.
Count after year-end: + cost of net sales, − purchases received. Count before: the reverse.
Goods on approval stay with the sender; consignment goods belong to the consignor.
traps: Don't value stock at selling price or MRP.
Don't add recoverable GST to cost.
Don't compare total cost with total NRV.
Don't forget to convert sales to cost (mark-up on cost vs margin on sales).

viva.q: What is meant by inventory? Give the types of inventory in a manufacturing concern.
viva.model: Inventory means assets kept for selling in the normal course of business, assets in the process of production for such sale, and materials or supplies to be consumed in production or in rendering services. A manufacturer holds raw materials, work in progress, finished goods, and stores, spares and loose tools.

viva.q: On what basis are inventories valued, and why?

viva.q: Which costs are included in the cost of inventory, and which are excluded?
viva.model: Cost includes the cost of purchase, such as purchase price, non-recoverable taxes and freight inward, less trade discounts; costs of conversion such as direct labour and production overheads; and other costs to bring the goods to their present location and condition. Excluded are abnormal wastage, storage costs unless needed in production, administrative overheads not related to production, selling and distribution costs, and taxes that are recoverable like GST credit.

viva.q: Explain FIFO and the weighted average method. Why is LIFO not permitted?
viva.model: Under FIFO the goods received first are issued first, so closing inventory is made up of the latest purchases. Under the weighted average method, the total cost of goods available is divided by the total units available, and under perpetual records a new average is worked out after every receipt. LIFO is not permitted because it rarely matches the actual flow of goods and leaves old outdated costs in the balance sheet.

viva.q: Distinguish between the periodic and the perpetual inventory systems.
viva.model: In the periodic system inventory is found by physical count at the end of the period, and cost of goods sold is the balancing figure, so losses are hidden in cost of goods sold. In the perpetual system a stores ledger records every receipt and issue continuously, cost of goods sold is known directly and closing inventory is the balancing figure, which allows inventory control.

viva.q: What is the effect on profit if closing inventory is overstated, and if opening inventory is overstated?

cases.title: Hira Stationers — choosing a cost formula
cases.case: Hira Stationers keeps periodic records for its premium notebooks. Opening inventory on 1 April 2026: 100 units @ ₹40. Purchases: June 300 units @ ₹42; October 150 units @ ₹44. Sales during the year were 350 units at ₹60 each. On 31 March 2027, 200 units are in stock; their net realisable value is ₹45 each.

mcqs.q: The periodic weighted average cost per unit (to two decimals) is:
mcqs.explain: Goods available cost 4,000 + 12,600 + 6,600 = 23,200 for 550 units; 23,200 ÷ 550 = ₹42.18. ₹42.00 is the simple average of the three prices (quantities ignored); ₹42.67 leaves out the opening inventory.

mcqs.q: Cost of goods sold under FIFO is:
Applying lower of cost and NRV to the FIFO figure, inventory is shown at:
mcqs.explain: NRV = 200 × 45 = ₹9,000, which is above FIFO cost ₹8,700, so cost is taken.
